column2: Act Fourteen
Crime and Punishment
Crime & Punishment

It had come alive. Hearts seemed to be beating inside the case—not one heart but seven. All seven blades awoke together, their different heartbeats mingling, some like great bells, others like urgent drums. This was an orchestra of violence, fit to accompany a story like the Tang tale of Liu Yi.
Late at night, on the top floor of the principal’s office.

One desk lamp, seven bone-china cups. Seven figures surrounded the enormous desk, sitting in the darkness beyond the lamplight. Wind rolled fallen leaves across the roof, sounding like countless ninjas stealing overhead. No one had spoken for a long time. The atmosphere shifted mysteriously, like the white steam spilling from the tea.
Anjou raised his cup to the others. “A rare pleasure indeed, inviting three students to our evening tea at once. Welcome, all of you, and your hardworking advisers...”

“Goddammit! Why do I have to go on a mission with a lunatic? Have I given up on my life of repeating grades? I’m not going! Absolutely not!” Someone plainly had no intention of playing along with the principal’s gracious manner. He squirmed in his chair and shouted.
Cassell College’s one and only G-rank student, Fingel von Frings. The reason he could only squirm instead of getting up and fleeing was that someone had tied his hands behind the chair with a belt.
Beside him, the vice principal held up his pants and grinned viciously.
“I haven’t even mentioned sending you to China to slay a dragon yet. Could you save your outburst for a little later?” Anjou scratched his head.

“Don’t think I can’t guess what you’re up to! Evening tea, my ass! This is a pep rally, right? You’re tying me and Chu Zihang to the same sinking ship, right? I’ve already done my job, Principal. You can’t go back on your word! Next year I graduate in a blaze of glory, become an Executive Department agent, and fly around the world on missions with sexy younger girls from school! Speeding down Cuban highways smoking cigars, lying on Hawaiian beaches while someone rubs sunscreen on me, rowing down the Mekong with some Asian girl I just happened to meet... My good times are almost here! Come on, I’ve spent nine years slogging toward graduation! I don’t want to die just before dawn!” Fingel was outraged and grief-stricken.

“You’re describing James Bond’s life, not an Executive Department agent’s,” Schneider, head of the department, rasped. “If anyone in my department lives that way, it can only mean I’ve failed to maintain discipline!”
“Can’t you leave a little room for imagination?” Fingel sighed.

“As the one and only G-rank, you think graduating will be that easy? Even if the principal and I let you slide, do you think the Board of Trustees won’t take its revenge? We’re creating an opportunity for you. Imagine how impressive your internship report will look if you finish this mission. The trustees won’t have a single excuse to stop you graduating! Otherwise, you may very well become the first tenth-year student in history!” The vice principal clapped Fingel hard on the shoulder, applying both carrot and stick to this stubborn mule.

“Better chewing pork knuckles in my tenth year than getting killed by this maniac’s indiscriminate Sovereign Flame!” Fingel glared at Chu Zihang beside him, though he had clearly lost some of his bluster.
Chu Zihang sat expressionlessly, drinking tea and eating chocolate cake.
“Violence is the only thing that works on this sort,” the vice principal told Guderian beside him.
Guderian nodded repeatedly, keenly aware of how much he still had to learn from the vice principal as an educator.

Anjou coughed. “May I continue? Inviting our finest students to drink black tea, discuss the college’s history, and look toward the future has been a tradition of ours for many years. The three students here tonight are the true elite of this institution. It is my great honor to inform you that you will be dispatched to China as trainee agents to investigate the recently exposed incident of a Dragon King’s awakening.”
“Your great honor can kiss my ass...” Fingel looked miserable.
“It won’t be just the three of us, will it?” Lu Mingfei felt uneasy too.

He had always heard that the Executive Department was packed with formidable fighters. Even among the professors who looked too frail to truss a chicken, plenty were terrifying monsters with offensive Yanling. Yet somehow two dragon-slaying missions in a row had landed on him, an underclassman. At least last time Manstein had led the team. This time the college seemed intent on making a team out of three students.

“The college is sending many teams. Yours will have only three members,” Anjou said. “Don’t think you lack experience. You are A-rank and S-rank—even Fingel was once A-rank. Your bloodlines give you an advantage over most Executive Department agents. The more exalted the ancient dragon you face, the more important your bloodline becomes.”

“The public disclosure of a Dragon King’s awakening is the greatest crisis in the college’s history. In fact, every elite agent the Executive Department can mobilize has been divided among teams and sent out,” Schneider said. “We’re also sending two student teams. The other consists of Caesar Gattuso, Chen Motong, and Xia Mi.”
Oh, so I finally don’t have to be the third wheel this time? Lu Mingfei thought. Maybe the college had kept them apart on purpose. Otherwise it would have been awkward for everyone.

The indignant Fingel froze. His eyes darted around, then he craned his neck and made faces at Lu Mingfei and Chu Zihang. “You two really are tragic! Both your crushes are on Caesar’s team! Maybe I should have a crush on Caesar. Then all three people we’re secretly in love with would be on the same team, and our tragedy squad would reach peak tragedy!” He turned and shouted at Anjou again. “Principal, isn’t this division of manpower a little uneven? They’ve got three A-ranks, two of them upperclassmen, every one of them able to handle things alone. We get one violent thug dragging two deadweights?”

“You mustn’t look at it that way. Their team has a first-year, a third-year, and a fourth-year. Yours has a second-year, a third-year, and you, a ninth-year. Yours is the senior team,” Anjou said mildly.
“Hey! You can’t count it like that!” Fingel protested. “That makes me worth all three of them put together!”
Without a word, the vice principal tightened the belt around Fingel’s wrists.

“Joking aside, sending Caesar was not my decision. It was the board’s,” Anjou said. “Chu Zihang’s bloodline remains ‘in question,’ and the board insisted on an additional team. Caesar chose Chen Motong and Xia Mi himself.”

“That’s blatant girlfriend poaching, isn’t it?” Fingel stared into Chu Zihang’s eyes and said earnestly, “I’m not one to stir things up, but let me tell you straight, junior: if someone tried stealing my girl, I’d fight him to the death, no matter what!”
Chu Zihang did not answer. He gazed at the light as though his mind had been wandering the whole time.

“All right, all right. Look who I’m stuck with: a wimp and a guy with facial paralysis.” Deciding that no one would respond however much he fussed, Fingel heaved a long sigh. “So do we at least get some kick-ass equipment? Like how Q always gives 007 some top-of-the-line stuff before a mission? An Aston Martin with an alchemical autocannon, a submarine that can drive down Chang’an Avenue—the more the better! Principal, unleash that evil Equipment Department of yours! Your good students are about to risk life and limb. If you’ve got any treasures stashed away, now’s not the time to hold out on us!”

“Unfortunately, the Equipment Department is one of the most difficult departments to deal with. Like the Executive Department, it answers both to me and to the board. And because of the board’s impeachment proceedings against me, I cannot intervene for the moment.” Anjou shrugged. “So you will not have the Equipment Department’s full support, as you did during Operation Bronze.”

“Are you kidding? At least then we had the Moniach and a Shkval torpedo with an alchemical warhead. This time you’re sending us in naked? Wow! Fingernails and teeth? Bite the Dragon King to death?” Fingel was dumbfounded. All evening he had been in a state of hysteria, falling apart again and again.
“Although my authority has been temporarily suspended, there are still some things I can call upon.” Anjou nodded to the vice principal.

The vice principal hauled a heavy black case from beneath the desk and set it on top. It was an aluminum-alloy case 180 centimeters long, with a black outer covering and steel-reinforced corners. A metal plate at one corner bore the inscription S20100144. An item from the Ice Cellar—one of the highest grade, its designation beginning with S. The numbers meant it was the 144th item added to the Ice Cellar’s collection in 2010.
Lu Mingfei immediately knew what it was. He could almost feel that dangerous thing’s long, slow breathing through the aluminum alloy.

The principal and vice principal each took out a bronze-colored key, inserted them simultaneously into locks on opposite sides of the case, and turned them together. Gears whispered inside. Interlocking metal teeth slowly withdrew. A narrow gap sprang open, and black-gold light spilled along it. For a moment even the desk lamp seemed to dim.
The principal lifted the lid. “The alchemical blades: Seven Deadly Sins.”
Apart from the principal, the vice principal, and Lu Mingfei, no one present had seen the set before. They all craned their necks at once.
“What’s this thing?” Fingel reached out and tapped the exquisitely ornamented blade case.

The vice principal flipped up a concealed latch. With a clear, ringing note, the inner mechanism slid out, bringing with it seven blades of completely different designs. In the lamplight, their black-gold edges revealed patterns like threads of ice, pine needles, drifting clouds, and flames. The vice principal drew a blade: a two-handed, long-handled weapon a full meter and a half long, its edge gracefully curved, its thickness about that of a finger.
“The design resembles a Chinese horse-chopping saber of the Song dynasty. It was named for its ability, wielded with both hands at full force, to take off a horse’s head.”
With a shhk, he drove the enormous blade into the desk.
“Hey! That desk is an antique, hand-carved by nineteenth-century Venetian craftsmen!” Anjou shouted.
“Oh. Got carried away.” The vice principal smiled apologetically. “Have someone replace the top for you.”

He drew another blade, a curved sword almost 1.2 meters long, its body slender, its cutting tip shaped like the prow of a longship. “Similar to a Japanese tachi of the Heian period. This design evolved from the Chinese Tang sword. A small point, narrow toward the tip and broad toward the base. A fine, classical shape.”
Another shhk. This sword, too, sank half a foot into the desktop.

“A yataghan, a type of Damascus blade, historically forged by Turkish swordsmiths. The authentic craft has now been lost. Its distinguishing feature is the reverse curve of its edge, while the tip straightens out, combining the advantages of saber and sword. Wielded with one hand.”
Shhk.
“A Han sword design, a straight blade with an octagonal cross section, also called a Han eight-faceted sword. An elegant thrusting weapon.”
Shhk.
Anjou covered his eyes and listened to seven successive sounds of metal piercing wood. Each meant another drop in the value of his precious antique.

The desk now bristled with blades. Within minutes, this scholarly private library had become a forbidding museum of edged weapons, gathering the killing instruments of many ages under one roof. Circling the desk, the vice principal flicked the horse-chopping saber with a bent finger. Its humming filled the room. The other six weapons resonated in response, forming a perfect scale.

“Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku first found this set in the City of Bronze. Lu Mingfei and Chen Motong found it a second time on Ye Sheng’s remains. It was lost again, then turned up at an invitation-only auction, where the college paid a great deal to buy it back. Each blade bears a different Draconic inscription. We cannot decipher the Draconic, but fortunately there is also ancient Hebrew, very likely the names of the seven weapons: Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Greed, Gluttony, and Lust.”
“The Seven Deadly Sins of Christianity,” Guderian said. “In Latin, superbia, invidia, ira, accidia, avaritia, gula, and luxuria. Together they form a medieval Latin word: saligia.”

“All the blades are forged from regenerated metal. The material looks identical, yet each has a different rigidity and toughness. This is alchemy at its highest level: creating new metals according to one’s will. Every master alchemist can only look up to such skill. It belongs solely to the supreme master of alchemy among the Four Monarchs, the King of Bronze and Fire,” Anjou said.

“The Four Monarchs command different powers. The King of Earth and Mountain, for example, is believed to possess the greatest might. The King of Bronze and Fire, meanwhile, is called the Throne of Alchemy, because only he commands flames hot enough to reach alchemy’s ultimate limits,” the vice principal said. “The craftsmanship of these seven weapons is astonishing. You could say they possess every virtue of every edged weapon in history. Combined, those virtues produce unparalleled killing power. Using them to kill humans would be like shooting flies with antiaircraft guns. So why would a Dragon King go to such trouble to forge them?”
“To kill his own kind,” Lu Mingfei said silently, looking at the row of cutting edges.

Lu Mingze had told him that, and he had never doubted it. The instant he saw these blades, he had dimly sensed the bloody destiny they carried. When Nono had taken them off Ye Sheng’s bones without a moment’s hesitation, a faint voice in Lu Mingfei’s heart had said, No... no... no...

Something that must never be touched. A gate of slaughter that must never be opened. A demonic seal that must never be removed... He thought Ye Sheng had died in that bronze city precisely because he had taken these blades away.

“We believe they were forged to kill the other first-generation dragons,” Anjou said softly. “Seven weapons, each corresponding to a weakness of one of the seven kings. Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Greed, Gluttony, Lust. With his supreme achievement in alchemy, Norton would pass judgment on his seven brothers. The ancient Hebrew on the outside of the case translates as: ‘All royal blood shall end by the sword!’”

“Come on. None of the Dragon Kings sounds particularly horny. Was Lust specially forged for you, Principal?” Fingel said. “And why would he kill the other Dragon Kings? Shouldn’t they team up and wipe us out first?”

“Dragons are a race that believes absolutely in power. Their familial affection is nothing beside their reverence for strength. If they believe a brother is too weak to deserve existence, they will start a war without hesitation, destroy him, and devour him. Both the rise and fall of the dragons stem from this savage tradition. Dragons are forever royalty. A king’s destiny is to be killed by a new king. That is how they pass on their power,” Anjou said.
“So when he forged these weapons, he had already begun counting down his younger brother’s life?” Chu Zihang asked.
Anjou nodded.
“And yet he was enraged when we killed his brother?”

“That is how strange the dragons are. They savagely devour their own kind, yet feel an anguish carved into their bones when one of their kind dies. Legend says that after the Black King devoured the White King, he roared in agony and flew to the highest point of the heavens, then plunged into the deepest ocean, smashing through the hard ice of winter. He repeated this seven times,” Anjou said.
“Sounds like a seriously messed-up artsy kid,” Fingel muttered. “But can these things really kill a Dragon King? Especially this little one... Can it even pierce dragon scales?”
“Not yet. Because what you’re seeing is not the true Seven Deadly Sins.” The vice principal pulled the blades out one by one and fitted them back into the case.
He bit open his finger, holding it upright so everyone could see the drop of blood, then slowly smeared it across the case. The blood quickly filled its engraved inscriptions.
“Stand back a little. It’s waking up.” The vice principal motioned everyone away.

They were already backing away without being told. Everyone could feel the change. It had come alive. Hearts seemed to be beating inside the case—not one heart but seven. All seven blades awoke together, their different heartbeats mingling, some like great bells, others like urgent drums. This was an orchestra of violence, fit to accompany a story like the Tang tale of Liu Yi: amid song and graceful dancing in Dongting Lake, the red dragon named Qiantang swept three thousand li through the sky, killed six hundred thousand people, destroyed eight hundred mu of crops, and devoured the young dragon who had treated his wife so heartlessly. Then, back in the blink of an eye, he donned his lofty hat and broad sash once more and greeted his guests with a smile.
Dark red, vine-like patterns emerged on the surface of the case, like blood vessels. Its beating hearts were pumping frenzied blood through its entire body.

Cold sweat covered Lu Mingfei’s forehead. He remembered the scene beneath the waters of the Three Gorges. This was exactly how the blades had been then. Holding them was like holding a dragon’s body! This was their true form. They had to be awakened with blood.
“Now try drawing the blades again. Mingfei first,” the vice principal said.

Lu Mingfei was deeply reluctant to go near the thing. No normal person would want to approach a vicious weapon poised between living and dead. Fortunately, though... this would not be his first time drawing these weapons. He was the one who had actually used them, but he could not say so. Obediently, he went to the desk, opened the hidden latch, drew a deep breath, and gripped the smallest blade, Lust, shaped like a Japanese wakizashi. Another force inside the case held the short sword in a death grip. Lu Mingfei’s face reddened as he strained with every ounce of strength he possessed. Suddenly he lost his balance and tumbled to the floor, clutching the freed blade.

“First stage passed. Keep going. Try the others,” the vice principal said. “Once awakened, this set develops an extremely powerful magnetic force holding the blades inside the case. The larger they are, the harder they are to draw.”
“I really can’t.” Lu Mingfei shook his head. “That nearly killed me already.”
“Try again.” The vice principal’s tone allowed no refusal. “The second blade. Gluttony!”

Lu Mingfei gripped the yataghan’s hilt. This time the force inside the case was easily ten times what it had been for Lust. The blade slowly emerged, but after drawing it only an inch, Lu Mingfei ran out of strength and sat on the floor panting.
“Keep going. Greed,” the vice principal said mildly.
“Hey, I couldn’t even get the second-smallest one out!” Lu Mingfei’s eyebrows drooped.
“Give it a try. Trying won’t kill you. At worst you’ll sprain an arm or something. No slacking! Slacking costs grade points!” the vice principal threatened viciously.

Greed barely cleared its sheath before being sucked back inside. Sloth lived up to its name and stayed thoroughly idle in the case, giving only a slight tremor amid Lu Mingfei’s shouts of exertion. The Han eight-faceted sword called Pride, the tachi called Envy, and the mighty horse-chopping saber called Wrath remained completely motionless. By the end Lu Mingfei had even jumped onto the desk and planted his feet on the case to pull, perfectly illustrating the saying about an ant trying to shake a great tree.
“That’s enough. Next, Fingel.” The vice principal clapped his hands.

Freed from his bonds, Fingel smugly rolled up his sleeves and showed Lu Mingfei biceps like lumps of iron. He really did have a strong pair of arms. He managed to draw every blade up through Greed, brandishing the Scottish broadsword with a look of immense satisfaction. Beyond that, however, he ran into the same wall as Lu Mingfei.
“Last, Chu Zihang,” the vice principal said. “Treat it as an exam. Give it everything you have.”

“Yes.” Chu Zihang went to the desk and breathed slowly. His arms were not as powerful as Fingel’s, but his specialized physical training was in tai chi. The explosive power born of suppleness could be several times greater than brute force alone.

He drew Lust as casually as pulling chopsticks from a sleeve. For Gluttony he sank into a horse stance, focused on his lower abdomen, and succeeded on his first attempt. Fingel no longer looked so smug. He had spent quite a while grunting and straining earlier. Chu Zihang adjusted his grip on Greed’s hilt and concentrated his mind. His long, steady breath seemed to flow all the way to his fingertips. He pulled!

Blood dripped onto the desk. Chu Zihang stood beside it, silently studying his palm. Both Lu Mingfei and Fingel were stunned. They had assumed he could draw at least as far as Wrath. Judging from his performance with the first two blades, he still had strength to spare. But the Scottish broadsword had not moved an inch inside its case. The dense metal scales on its hilt had opened and pierced his palm. Only when he took his hand away did the scales slowly close.
Greed had rejected him.
“Exam over. Dismissed!” The vice principal snapped his fingers. “Schneider, Guderian, Mingfei, Fingel—come with me. The principal needs a word with the student who failed.”
The door closed. Chu Zihang was still looking at his palm. He was proud. A-rank. Some believed he had surpassed A-rank and was approaching S. Yet these weapons had rejected him. Mercilessly.
Anjou tossed him his pocket square. “It was a bloodline test.”
Chu Zihang wrapped the cloth around his hand and nodded. “I understand.”
“Fingel drew the third blade, but you were rejected. Why?”
“Because my bloodline isn’t as pure as people think,” Chu Zihang said softly. “My blood was cleansed. For a month, it won’t return to its original purity.”

Anjou nodded. “Yes. Most people at this college think you’re beyond A-rank. They think your bloodline is purer than Caesar’s, that you deserve the distinction of S-rank far more than Mingfei. But you know the truth. Your bloodline’s purity doesn’t even reach A-rank. A careful study of your parents makes that clear. Your father may have been a very rare sort of hybrid, but your mother is entirely human. Their child would be unlikely to be an even more exceptional hybrid. Mingfei’s parents, on the other hand, are both hybrids. You have those golden eyes that never go out because you mastered blood amplification. You forcibly raised your bloodline’s purity. Being unable to control your golden eyes is a sign that your bloodline is nearing the point of going out of control. I don’t know how far you are from your final degeneration, but if you restrain yourself, you can prolong your life.”
Chu Zihang nodded.
“You know you probably don’t have very long to live, don’t you?” Anjou sighed.

“By the time I discovered the problem, it was too late,” Chu Zihang said quietly. “You were right, Principal. Blood amplification is an abyss of a technique. From the first day I used it, I was already sliding down.”
“So you never disclosed the technique to anyone.”
“That’s right.”

Anjou tossed a file in front of Chu Zihang. “We know about the incident involving your father on July 3, 2007. It remains a mystery to this day. But if you want to find out what happened, first you have to stay alive.”
“I understand.” Chu Zihang gave a soundless smile. “Everyone wants to live.”
“Do you know about the Nibelungen Project?”
Chu Zihang shook his head.
“You didn’t obtain all the information on blood amplification.”
Chu Zihang froze, then snapped his head up.

“There is indeed a way to increase the purity of a hybrid’s dragon blood. It is an alchemical technique whose safeguards prevent the higher proportion of dragon blood from rewriting the hybrid’s genes. But it is enormously costly and can be used on only one person. The Nibelungen Project screens unsafe bloodlines out of the college while also selecting a candidate whom it will help complete an ‘evolution,’” Anjou said slowly. “I believe you understand how much such a gift would mean to you. It is the only way to safely cross the critical blood threshold and realize the full potential of dragon blood. It is also your only way to survive.”
“Such a technique exists?” Chu Zihang’s eyes widened.

“It does. And you are on the list of candidates.” Anjou waved a hand. “Go. You need an achievement to compete with Caesar for that place. He has killed a Dragon King. You should make an equal contribution.”
“Understood!” Chu Zihang hesitated, looking at Anjou as he sat quietly drinking tea beneath the lamp. “Thank you.”
“No need.” Anjou smiled and raised his cup.
“One last thing.” Chu Zihang stopped at the door. “If Fingel really doesn’t want to go, I don’t think we should force him.”

“Do you really think that man is deadweight? You’re wrong. Fingel von Frings was once an A-rank student here. He took part in many missions and is the most experienced agent among the students. There is only one reason he stopped taking assignments: he was badly injured on a mission, badly enough to affect his mind. What you see now is not his true self... Granted, he was always rather outrageous... but not like this. Ten years ago, I saw him much as I see you now.” Anjou drew from his sleeve the folding knife he always carried and tossed it down from the upper level. Chu Zihang caught it.

“I’m lending it to you. It can wound first-generation dragons. When the yataghan handed down through my friend Meinhard’s family broke, we forged this from a fragment of its tip. It’s a precious memento.” Anjou gave a convincing military salute. “Remember to return it when you’re done.”
“Yes, General.” Chu Zihang imitated him and returned the salute.

The door closed, and someone emerged through a side door. The vice principal had come back. He drew up a chair and sat beside the desk. “Now we can finally prove that Lu Mingfei’s bloodline fully deserves its S-rank.”

“Yes. In fact, he could have drawn all the way through Sloth. Fingel and Chu Zihang failed because the blades rejected them. In Lu Mingfei’s case...” Anjou did not know whether to laugh or cry. “He simply wasn’t strong enough.”

The vice principal sighed. “The blades had clearly accepted him. They were moving inside the case, yet that magnetic pull kept them from coming out. Even weapons inhabited by living spirits must find that depressing.”
“At least he is the most suitable wielder of the Seven Deadly Sins we have found so far,” Anjou said. “We just need to add a few physical-training classes to his schedule.”
“But drawing only four isn’t enough, is it? The last three are the real killing weapons.” The vice principal frowned.
“Perhaps we should let Caesar try next time?” Anjou smiled.
“Why don’t you try yourself?”

Anjou gently stroked the case. “I’m a little afraid. Afraid to learn my limits. Afraid to discover there are things I cannot do... I must believe I am a man capable of anything. The man who will lay the dragons to rest cannot be a man with limits!”

Meanwhile, the hall of Amber Hall blazed with light. Caesar had rented the campus villa as both the Student Council’s headquarters and his own residence. After renovations, it looked more like a royal retreat. Black cases covered a table in the center of the dance floor. Their lids opened one after another, displaying all manner of equipment. No normal person could ever guess what any of it did merely by looking... Even with manuals, using it would be dangerous, because none of these things had been developed by normal people...
Cassell College’s Equipment Department had made its grand entrance.

Researchers crowded around the table adjusting the equipment, while Caesar inspected it with his new teammate Xia Mi, like an emperor arriving at his summer palace with his favorite consort for a holiday.
When Caesar received Norma’s notification about the China mission, these researchers with their black cases were already waiting outside Amber Hall.
“What’s this?” Caesar noticed a researcher polishing an exquisite brass blowtorch.

The researcher gave him a contemptuous glance, turned the blowtorch sideways, and pressed a hidden button. A blazing jet of fire a full twenty meters long flashed out and vanished. Searing wind struck their faces. It was hard to imagine such a flame coming from a pipe only two centimeters across. The other researchers carried on with their work. Playing with fire in a crowd was hardly outrageous for an Equipment Department known as the “Happy Camp for Lunatics.” Anyone who lacked that kind of composure would never survive there.

“We call it dragon's breath. Right now it’s loaded only with chemical fuel, but you can also fill it with nitroglycerin and mercury. Its flames can inflict fatal damage on third-generation dragons. If you encounter a first-generation dragon...” The researcher paused. “It can also serve as a flashlight.”
“Impressive.” Caesar smiled and nodded.
“A combat helmet with a metal faceplate. Besides providing strong protection, it can amplify your biting force when you chew.”
“A lightly modified Vertu phone. Nothing particularly special, but you can throw it as a bomb.”
“Your passport. Chemically treated. Customs will never notice anything unusual, but in an emergency, add a fuse the size of a cigarette butt and it can serve as a bomb too.”
Caesar hesitated for a long time over this creation. “But if I burn my passport, how do I leave the country?”

“If you want to keep the passport, you can use the phone bomb instead. Or any of the other bombs.” The researcher was very impatient with the question. “There are about forty-five in the complete kit. We’ll give you a bomb inventory.”
“The lighter’s a bomb too, right?” Xia Mi had found a silver lighter, very much to Caesar’s taste: a heavy S. T. Dupont with a ringing metal lid.

“Anyone could guess that a lighter might be turned into a bomb. If we did that, we wouldn’t be the Equipment Department.” The researcher gave a smug, chilly smile. “We only added an MP3 player! With a built-in speaker!”

Using a fingernail, the researcher turned a screw in the base and set the lighter on the table. The little silver thing began playing an aria from Puccini’s Madama Butterfly. It was a fresh and oddly delicate sensation: a silver lighter vibrating faintly as it sang “One Fine Day” at the top of its voice, expressing all the tenderness of a Japanese woman waiting for her husband. The sound was bright, joyous, and superbly clear.
Pink hearts lit up in Xia Mi’s eyes. She snatched up the lighter. “Can I keep this?”
Caesar shrugged. “Of course. Would you like that shoulder-fired sniper cannon too?”

“I’ll pass.” Xia Mi happily played with the lighter. A thin, sharp tongue of fire shot out, a full seventy centimeters long. No other lighter in the world burned so fiercely. It was practically a lightsaber!
Watching her rabbit-like figure and bouncing long hair, Caesar thought that this girl was either astonishingly oblivious or exactly the sort of lunatic who belonged in the Equipment Department.

He came up behind Xia Mi. Much taller than she was, he had to bend halfway down to speak by her ear, as if teasing a little girl. “Helping Chu Zihang once doesn’t mean I’m his friend. A rival is always a rival. Doesn’t it worry you, accepting gifts from the enemy?”

“I’m here as an undercover agent.” Xia Mi put the lighter away, picked up a plate, and buried her face in cake, getting strawberry jam even on the corners of her mouth. “Don’t you know I’m Chu Zihang’s rumored girlfriend?”
“I know, I know.” Caesar could only nod.

“Besides this equipment, there is one special item. The Board of Trustees specifically instructed us to place it in your hands.” A man in a black uniform, quite unlike the other researchers, had come up behind Caesar. He too carried a black case, but had not put it on the table and opened it with the rest.
Caesar glanced at him, then smiled at Xia Mi. “Want to see something interesting?”
The study door closed, and the last black case was opened. Inside lay an exquisite crossbow with a single bolt. Its enormous, decidedly un-aerodynamic head was a prism of crystal glass.
“Ordinary crystal glass, not some magic gemstone. But hold it up to the light,” the researcher in black suggested.
A dark red, blood-like thread extended through the synthetic quartz crystal, its surface shimmering with a crystalline gleam.
“A Philosopher’s Stone?” Caesar frowned.
“Not an ordinary Philosopher’s Stone. This one was refined from the remains of the Dragon King Constantine. One of only a few currently in existence,” the researcher said.

“In alchemical terms, a Philosopher’s Stone is pure spirit element. What difference does it make whether it comes from a Dragon King’s bones or somewhere else? Gold from an Egyptian pharaoh and gold freshly dug from an Ethiopian mine are no different once you refine them into pure gold bars.”
“There is a difference. This one is less pure,” the researcher said.
“Less pure?” Caesar blinked.

“There are some peculiar impurities we cannot remove, no matter what we try. But those impurities are precisely what makes it so different from an ordinary Philosopher’s Stone. For instance... it must not come into contact with oxygen. If it does, everything around it will burn with explosive speed. That’s why we sealed it inside the crystal.”
“Those impurities are...” Caesar looked straight into the researcher’s eyes.

“Fire element. Pure fire element. Alchemists have never devoted themselves to purifying fire element, because spirit element is more useful. It is the elixir of immortality and the stone that turns things to gold. They didn’t think fire element was particularly useful. It exists in every kind of flame, but cannot be captured and is constantly dispersing. This time, however, we captured fire element and sealed it with a Philosopher’s Stone. Only a Dragon King’s remains can produce a crystal like this. It is impure, but it holds a mixture of powers beyond human imagination.” The researcher paused. “It is a concept.”
“A concept?”

“Its concept is combustion. It releases something like a domain. As long as there is combustible matter within that domain, it will command that matter to burn as fast as possible. The result is an explosion. In theory, this combustion does not burn the substance itself, so it is not consumed. That makes the combustion endless! The principle is the same as a Yanling. Whoever releases a Yanling issues commands within its domain, and those commands can even alter the laws of physics. This substance approaches the fundamental nature of the world, or... the realm of God, if you like. Nothing we have, whether science or alchemy, can fully explain it. Perhaps the monarch of flame himself could have explained it. But he is dead.”
“Sounds like the spark that could destroy the world.” Caesar gently returned the bolt to its case.

“Don’t worry. This is specially made quartz glass. It absolutely won’t shatter if you drop it.” The researcher smiled. “This is the family’s greatest contribution to your mission. This kind of power can kill a first-generation dragon.”

Caesar raised an eyebrow. “Sounds like Prometheus, the thief of fire. Steal a thread of the King of Bronze and Fire’s power to kill the King of Earth and Mountain. Are you one of the family’s people?”

The researcher gave a cold smile. “Gattuso may be the most influential name on the Board of Trustees, but thinking you can claim the Equipment Department’s deputy director as one of your people is probably taking your self-confidence a little too far.”

“The Equipment Department’s deputy director? You?” Caesar’s pupils contracted sharply. He turned to stare at the thin, pale man. The Equipment Department had always stayed hidden underground; no one seemed to know who ran it. Whenever the college needed equipment support, these tech geeks in white lab coats and thick glasses emerged from their underground laboratories with cases, handed over the goods, and hastily offered a few words of explanation. Sometimes they did not even provide a manual, let alone training. Yet this time the department, usually too lazy to deal with outsiders, had sent someone as senior as its deputy director to make a delivery.

The deputy director could not be bothered to answer. He snapped the case shut and pushed it toward Caesar. “In the pentagram representing the five elements, earth is at the lower left and fire at the lower right. Draw the pentagram and you will find that no line connects those two elements. There is therefore no circuit of transformation between them. In the terminology of Chinese alchemy, neither generates nor overcomes the other. If the powers of fire and earth collide, it will be a collision of pure force, like two bullets fired at each other along the same trajectory. The consequences could be unimaginable. Use it cautiously.” He gave another cold smile. “But if you really face the King of Earth and Mountain, I suggest you not hesitate. He won’t give you much time for hesitation.”
The deputy director turned to leave, not even bothering to say goodbye.
“If you’re not one of the family’s people, why bring S-rank equipment like this here?” Caesar asked.

“As researchers, we don’t care whether the board or the principal runs this college. Our job is to extract the strongest power from anything we can, seal it with the best technology available, and watch the resulting weapon perform on the grandest stage.” The deputy director did not turn around. “Actually, I very much look forward to seeing you use that bolt in a crowded Chinese city center. Especially against an exalted Dragon King. A collision of pure forces. It ought to be beautiful, wouldn’t you say?”
“A crazy dad means one crazy kid. A crazy mom means a whole litter,” Xia Mi whispered to Caesar.

The deputy director heard her, but took no offense. He cackled like a crow spotting carrion and pushed the door open. He brushed past a girl standing outside with her hand raised to knock. He did not even look at her, as though she were nothing but air. Caesar’s expression, however, changed slightly when he saw her.
“Could you let us talk alone?” he asked Xia Mi with a smile, his tone indulgent, as though coaxing a child. “If you want cake, help yourself from the refrigerator.”
“Mm, how generous... No problem!” Xia Mi slipped past the girl. They exchanged a glance and polite little nods.
The girl sat on the sofa. She held a heavy envelope.
“You kept your word.” Caesar studied her appraisingly. “Would you like a drink?”

“No need. I just have to give you this.” The girl tossed the envelope to Caesar. “These are the materials I photocopied for Chu Zihang. They’re all parchment manuscripts kept by the Lionheart Society. Some are badly damaged.”

Caesar looked inside the envelope. Everything was handwritten in Old English, ancient Hebrew, or ancient Latin, accompanied by crude, puzzling illustrations like images on very old tarot cards: a hanging man, a burning tower, a pontiff with a skull-like face.

“Parchment manuscripts.” Caesar stroked the pages admiringly. “Wonderful things. In the Middle Ages, one parchment manuscript could buy a manor. A famous private collector of the time owned seven and took great pride in them. Together those books were worth a fortune. Scribes wrote on precious parchment, and when they were finished, the bones of their fingers were cut off and used to decorate the cover, signifying that there would never be a second copy. Texts accorded such treatment usually concerned witchcraft, alchemy, and black magic, so they were also books of the dead and books of demons. They say the Library of Alexandria held thirty thousand parchment scrolls before the Christian era, only for an Arab army to burn them all. Who knows how much occult knowledge of the dragons turned to ash that day? It pains me to think of it.” He looked straight at the girl. “What I want is in here?”
“Everything about blood amplification is in there. I can’t understand it, but you should be able to. You consider yourself his equal. He worked it out from these damaged records.”
Caesar nodded. “You really did keep your word. But Chu Zihang let you handle these because he trusted you. Does this count as betraying him?”

“That’s none of your business. Our bargain was that you would support Chu Zihang at the hearing and I would give you these photocopies.” The girl did not flinch from Caesar’s cold gaze. “Our transaction is complete. If there’s nothing else, I’ll go. I still have a paper to finish.” She rose and headed for the door.

“When he discovers he’s no longer the only person in the world who understands blood amplification, will he hate you?” Caesar admired her slender figure from behind. “It’s his treasure. You used it without asking him.”
“He’s just a messed-up kid who doesn’t know how to manage his own life,” the girl said impatiently.
“A messed-up kid?” Caesar stared. “The person I’ve always considered my rival is just a messed-up kid?”

The girl turned back, her dark eyes serious. “Yes. A messed-up kid. They aren’t all the same. When they feel helpless, some bawl their eyes out. Others stiffen their necks, lower their heads, and stubbornly keep going their own way. He’s the stubborn kind. But whichever kind they are, they all need someone to help them.”

“Aren’t you giving up a little too much for him?” Caesar leaned beside the window and looked out at the brightly lit work site in the ruins of the Foundation Well. The Equipment Department was working through the night, seemingly determined to send every cubic centimeter of soil to the lab for analysis. “I’m sorry. If I’d known you were coming now, I would have had Xia Mi wait in another room.”
“It’s all right. My liking him... and his liking me are two unrelated things.” The girl lowered her eyes.

“I’ll bring him back safely from China. With me there, he won’t even get to face the Dragon King. But whether he chooses Xia Mi or you afterward is none of my business. Some things... if I were you, I’d fight for them.” Caesar raised his glass. “Good night, Susie.”
“Take good care of Nono. She was very happy the night she received your proposal by text. But if you really mean to propose, you should bring a ring.” Susie closed the door behind her.
Rome, Italy.

Frost tossed the report he had finished reading onto his desk and sighed. “I never really expected to remove Anjou as principal this time. But if we could have found a problem with Chu Zihang, we could at least have shaken Anjou’s position. Yet Caesar... That child never seems to understand how much his family loves him.”
“It was my failure.” Parsi stood respectfully before the desk.
“It had nothing to do with you. You did everything you could, and you did well,” Frost reassured him gently. “Who posted the dragon-slaying bounty on Hunter Market? Any leads?”

“No. The account belongs to a veteran hunter, but reliable intelligence says he encountered sharks while vacationing in Tahiti several months ago. The sharks tore him apart and ate him. Since no remains were recovered, the police still list him as missing. For the same reason, Hunter Market did not immediately deactivate his account.”
“Such an unusual way to die. And then he rises like a ghost on Hunter Market to announce a dragon-slaying job to the entire world?” Frost smiled. “Our opponent is very bold.”
“Yes,” Parsi said. “It challenges the rule all hybrids follow: never reveal the dragons’ secret to humanity. But sir, is the information credible?”
“If only it were a rumor.” Frost was silent for a moment. “Unfortunately, it isn’t.”
“We’ve detected the awakening of the King of Earth and Mountain?” Parsi was startled.
“Yes. By monitoring the frequency of earthquakes.” Frost took out a map and spread it on the desk. It was a map of China, covered in densely packed markings.

“The awakening of one of the Four Monarchs is actually easier to detect than that of an ordinary dragon. Their power is so immense that each awakening brings something resembling a natural disaster. Our failure to detect the King of Bronze and Fire was an exception. The bronze city had sunk into the Three Gorges Reservoir, and the immense volume of water absorbed the heat of his awakening. When the tenured professors deduced that the one awakening this time was the King of Earth and Mountain, we began collecting seismic data from around the world. The ground is constantly moving. Small earthquakes happen every day. But if the frequency and intensity rise sharply in a particular region, then something unusual must be happening in the crust. All these marks are records of seismic activity. After running the calculations, we finally focused on this city.” Frost tapped the red five-pointed star in the middle of the map. “Beijing. A place the Chinese say is blessed with concentrated dragon energy. After passing through the Great Wall, China’s last dynasty, the Qing, inherited that capital from its enemies. It stands beside the Yan Mountains, believed to be the bones of an ancient dragon, extending east through Shanhai Pass. Beyond the pass lay the Manchus’ homeland. The Manchus followed the dragon through the pass and finally saw dense dragon energy above Beijing. These ideas are dismissed as absurd geomancy. But history always becomes legend. Now every clue is converging on that city. Something connected to the dragons may indeed be hidden there. Perhaps even... a real ancient dragon.”
“Have we begun operations in Beijing?” Parsi asked.

“We haven’t had time. What finally convinced us something was there was an incident a few days ago. We lost contact with two agents in Beijing. The family has always cultivated trusted people within the Executive Department. These agents have satellite tracking devices implanted in their molars. Even if they died, those devices should keep working.”
“The signals disappeared?”

“Not entirely. Roughly every two and a half minutes, both signals reappear. We don’t know why. The cause remains unclear. But something has undoubtedly happened to them. Before we lost contact, they called to give a warning. The call was forcibly cut off. We haven’t been able to reach them since.”
Parsi thought for a moment. “If the signals appear every two and a half minutes in a repeating cycle, they may be on something moving in a loop. Though we can’t be certain they’re still alive.”

“We’ll leave that for Caesar to find out. We’re sending Caesar’s team, and Anjou is sending Chu Zihang’s. This is direct competition over the choice of candidate for the Nibelungen Project. But the ultimate honor must belong to Caesar. Fenrisulfr, the King of Earth and Mountain, will be the second dragon to die by Caesar’s hand. And we must obtain his remains!”
“Understood. But our intelligence is very limited this time. The situation is nowhere near as clear as it was for the Three Gorges operation. I’m afraid Caesar won’t know where to begin,” Parsi said.

“That is why we equipped him with a Philosopher’s Stone refined from a Dragon King’s bones.” Frost smiled. “It is a weapon, and it is bait. It is the blood of a Dragon King. Every dragon will smell its powerful scent. They will come to Caesar. The King of Earth and Mountain will be no exception.”
Parsi’s expression changed. “But Caesar doesn’t know...”

“There is no need to worry about him. Caesar is the one the family has awaited for centuries,” Frost said softly. “He merely needs tempering. We will never let him die young. He is the one we have chosen to usher in a new age!”

The family had produced descendants with far purer bloodlines than Caesar’s. The many high-risk Yanling they displayed were recorded, but they were not raised as heirs. Instead, their names were quietly removed from the family tree, and they were secretly sent overseas like freaks. Decades of waiting had brought only disappointment after disappointment, until the family elders received that silent infant from a nurse’s bloodstained hands. The baby did not cry. From the moment he left the womb, his ice-blue eyes were open, observing the world.
“His name shall be Caesar, the name of a great ruler in Italy’s history.” The elders stroked the infant as though he were a priceless treasure. “He is the one we have waited a thousand years for.”

Caesar Gattuso. A bloodline chosen from a thousand, from ten thousand, from a hundred thousand. Even with his pride, Caesar could scarcely imagine his own future. It was too vast, too magnificent, reaching far beyond the age in which he lived.
The pity was that he would not obey!

Disobedient children were the most infuriating. Sometimes, looking at that stubborn face, you really wanted to slap it. But what good would a slap do? Even if you split his cheek and sent threads of blood into his eyes, those ice-blue pupils would not so much as blink. They would regard you with contempt. That was true stubbornness: stubbornness unto death.
“They all have their rebellious phase.” Frost sighed.

Midnight, Chicago International Airport. A Boeing 747-400 airliner waited for its transoceanic flight. Only red-eyes were flying at this hour. The apron was silent as a shuttle bus delivered the passengers beneath the wing.

“Is this some kind of mistake? Why make us take a shuttle to the middle of nowhere to board?” Fingel complained loudly. “Aren’t we traveling on official business? Why economy? If we can’t have first class, we should at least get business! We’re going off to die for humanity!”
“Apparently the other flights were sold out, so this is an overnight charter. Even these tickets weren’t easy to get. The last three seats in economy,” Chu Zihang said mildly.
“And they didn’t give priority to Caesar’s team?” Fingel sounded a little pleased. “Looks like they really value us this time!”
“I heard Caesar requisitioned one of his family’s Gulfstream business jets. They took off an hour ago.”

“Huh? Shouldn’t you be saying that through gritted teeth? You look like a rich kid too. Aren’t you ashamed that you’re a poor rich kid while Caesar’s a rich rich kid? You don’t even feel the slightest urge to fight him to the death!” Fingel delivered his verdict gravely. “Without that fighting spirit, I think our team is going to lose.”
“My dad was just someone’s driver.” Expressionlessly, Chu Zihang handed over his boarding pass.
The flight attendant smiled like a flower, took the pass, tore it, and returned half to Chu Zihang. “Welcome. A new face.”
Chu Zihang met her eyes through his sunglasses. After a few seconds of silence, he nodded. “I see. Hello.”

The Boeing 747-400’s enormous cabin was packed. It looked like a charter for a tour group. The passengers all seemed to know one another. Some chatted, some entertained children in neighboring seats, and others leafed through newspapers and magazines.
“These seats are tiny,” Fingel muttered, stealing glances at a beautiful woman nearby with her hair in a high bun.

Lu Mingfei was a little surprised. He had never thought of Fingel as particularly burly. The man always wore a loose, oversized shirt and walked hunched over, giving the impression of someone rather sickly. But squeezed into an economy seat, he turned out to be a very substantial lump indeed, filling every inch of it.

“It’s a direct flight. We’ll take the Bering Strait route, along the Arctic Circle. About fourteen hours.” Chu Zihang handed them two little packets, each containing an eye mask and earplugs. “Best to get some sleep. We start working as soon as we land.”
“Oh, wow. Such motherly care!” Fingel was delighted.

Lu Mingfei took the packet absently and quickly put on the mask and earplugs. He had been listless for days, yet his head kept flashing with all sorts of muddled thoughts he should not be thinking. Sleep would mean thinking less. The mask and earplugs seemed to seal him inside a private darkness. Dimly, he heard Fingel shout, “Hey, miss, when are you serving food? Do you have beer? Can I get two meals?”

Suddenly he remembered lying in darkness behind an eye mask like this at the end of summer, three months earlier. Rain had pattered against the plane’s skin. He had felt the phone in his pocket, wondering whether, in another half hour, someone might send him a birthday message.

The engagement and all that had probably already happened quietly by then, hadn’t it? He simply hadn’t known. So he had thought there was still a little hope, and on the plane he had even had that pathetic little dream.
“Hell! This seat’s going to snap my spine.” Muttering, Fingel pulled off his eye mask and stood to roll his shoulders.
The plane had climbed above the clouds. Outside lay heavy darkness, and the cabin lights were dim. Chu Zihang and Lu Mingfei slept side by side like corpses.

After a double helping of beer, the need to pee was inevitable. Fingel lurched upright and swayed toward the restroom, humming off-key rap. He stepped inside with a satisfied air, looked up, and opened his eyes so wide they nearly burst out of their sockets!

On the way to the restroom, his back had been to the passengers. Now he faced them. In the dim light he could clearly see faint golden pupils, like pairs of fireflies flying side by side. Even the sleeping brat had a pale golden glow seeping between his eyelids. An old man reading a newspaper noticed Fingel staring and lifted his head to give him a cold glance. In that instant the gold in his eyes blazed like blades!
“I must have a fever...” Fingel felt his forehead.
“Having trouble finding your seat, sir? Please go back and sit down. We’re in a high-speed air current.” The flight attendant’s gentle voice sounded behind him.

“You have no idea what kind of passengers you’re taking to China, do you, innocent little bunny?” Fingel muttered as he turned. He saw that the pretty flight attendant he had eyed several times had eyes... as richly golden as champagne beneath a gas lamp!
The attendant patted Fingel’s cheek and squeezed his slack jaw, smiling. “Handsome, don’t you know what kind of plane you’re on? People without the bloodline can’t board this flight.”
This was a flying... dragon’s nest!

Caesar woke in bed. Beyond the window lay utter darkness. This Gulfstream business jet happened to have three full-sized beds, enough for all three of them to rest. He checked his watch. Four hours until they reached China. They were over the Arctic Circle.
Caesar liked this jet very much. The firmness of the beds had been adjusted to his specifications. But he had not slept well. There had been an unease in his dreams, as if something were approaching.
He looked out the window for a long time. The blinking red light on the wing illuminated the clouds below, laying a wash of red across them like spilled blood.

He doubted he could get back to sleep. Opening the case he had brought aboard, he glanced at the crossbow and bolt. A thread of light flickered inside the synthetic crystal of the arrowhead. He took his laptop from the case, connected to the internet, and opened one of his frequently visited sites from his bookmarks: Hunter Market.

Very few people knew Caesar Gattuso’s other identity: he was a hunter. He had been one before entering Cassell College, registering an account on Hunter Market at fifteen. Of course, he had no need to work for bounties. Even the most generous would barely cover his private jet’s fuel and the tips he scattered so casually. He simply enjoyed a little adventure, and plenty of hunters were interesting people. His username was Governor of Gaul. The historical dictator Caesar had conquered Gaul.

The bounty on the Dragon King had been pinned to the top, with thousands of replies. Apparently many hybrids had accounts here. Formerly lurkers, they were all surfacing now. Some expressed surprise, some declared themselves unruffled by rumors, some speculated about how many people would rush to Beijing for the enormous reward, and some mingled with the crowd posting nonsense. It was as lively as a variety show. Apparently hybrids had at least inherited humanity’s appetite for gossip. Caesar scrolled down, skipping the junk and reading the replies that had value. This was not like Cassell College’s campus news site, where every account could be traced to a person. Some perfectly ordinary username might well conceal the leader of a family.
Caesar had no leads on the Dragon King either. He was pinning his hopes on this motley gathering of a website.
Suddenly he stopped. A post no one had replied to yet: “Information on the Dragon King for sale. US$200,000, payment up front.”

There were plenty of posts like this. Someone on Hunter Market was always trying to sell information, and almost all of it was false. They were like the advertising spam that regularly appeared on ordinary websites. Regulars naturally ignored them, their eyes passing over without so much as a flicker of brain activity. Yet for some reason, when Caesar saw this reply, his temple gave a faint throb. Something was off about it as an advertisement. He could not say what.
He reread it several times, weighing every word, but still could not find the strange point that troubled him. Deciding he was probably being a little oversensitive, he prepared to scroll on.
Then he saw the poster’s username: phoenix. The phoenix.

At last he understood what was wrong. He had never seen this username on the hunter site, yet a common name like phoenix should have been registered long ago. This was an old account that had been lurking for years. Had it surfaced merely to sell false information?

Caesar opened phoenix’s profile. Most profiles on the hunter site were blank, but phoenix had retained certain details. Its registration date, for example. It had registered twenty-three years earlier, when the global internet was still in its infancy and Hunter Market was probably some sort of test version. The account already existed then. It was the seventh account ever registered on the site.
Caesar considered for a moment, then sent phoenix a private message.

His attention was entirely on the screen, and he had not activated Kamaitachi. So he did not notice the dense, sea-like clouds beneath the fuselage beginning to boil. A black shadow rose, parting the vapor, and silently followed the Gulfstream. Farther below, on an enormous Arctic ice floe, the ice cracked and similar shadows emerged. The heavy blows of their takeoff shattered the floe. Groups of dark shapes followed beneath the business jet like fighter planes in formation.
Like a swarm of bloodthirsty bats.
